summary: This note is a Wikipedia-style overview of the history of science, moving through Indian, Hellenistic, Islamic, medieval European, Chinese, and modern developments. It covers advances in mathematics, medicine, astronomy, geology, seismology, economics, politics, evolution, and genetics. It also includes a critical passage on how modern textbooks represent the history of economics and Adam Smith's 'invisible hand'.
one_line: An overview of the history of science across civilizations, from ancient astronomy and medicine to plate tectonics, evolution, and genetics.
key_facts: Aryabhata (476-550) introduced sine, versine, cosine and inverse sine in his Aryabhatiya (499).
In 628 AD, Brahmagupta suggested that gravity was a force of attraction.
Arabic translations of Indian astronomers' texts introduced what would become Arabic numerals to the Islamic World by the 9th century.
Madhava of Sangamagrama is considered the "founder of mathematical analysis".
The Suśrutasamhitā of Suśruta is Ayurveda's most famous text and describes procedures including rhinoplasty, cataract surgery and perineal lithotomy.
Aristarchus of Samos was the first known person to propose a heliocentric model of the solar system.
The Antikythera mechanism (150-100 BC) was an analog computer for calculating the position of planets.
Adam Smith's An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations was published in 1776.
Ibn Sina (Avicenna) pioneered experimental medicine and was the first physician to conduct clinical trials.
Zhang Heng invented a seismometer in 132 CE that alerted authorities in Luoyang to an earthquake about 400-500 km northwest of the capital.
Charles Darwin put forward the theory of evolution by natural selection in On the Origin of Species in 1859.
By 1953, James D. Watson, Francis Crick and Maurice Wilkins clarified the basic structure of DNA.
A massive international effort to map the entire human genome (the Human Genome Project) began in 1990.
Since 1970, plate tectonics has served as the unifying principle in geology.
Pierre Duhem's thesis about the Catholic Church's Condemnation of 1277 led to the study of medieval science as a serious discipline.
